1:
The Psalter's second psalm opens with a startled question — why the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain — and the witnesses read the whole poem as a drama in four voices before they touch the first line. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe its architecture: a prophetic psalm in which the rebels, the LORD, and his Anointed each come forward and speak for themselves, while the framework is the poet's own discourse, like the chorus of a Greek drama; the Anointed who speaks in the middle is not the anonymous singer himself. Charles Ellicott presses the opening word, rendering it not simply 'rage' but 'why did the nations band together, or muster' — the Hebrew verb occurring only here, its cognates elsewhere of a festive crowd and of a conspiracy — and reads the parallel 'imagine' as 'meditate' or 'mutter,' the whispered treasons passing to and fro among the nations.

The reformed John Gill weighs whether the raging 'heathen' are the Jews, so called for their tribes, or the Gentiles, and decides for the Gentiles, as the apostles read it in Acts 4:25; the word for 'rage,' he says, intends a tumultuous gathering, as of a mob, with great confusion and noise. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the din as one great struggle over the kingdom of Christ, hell and heaven contesting it — princes and people, court and country, for once united against the Anointed, their opposition spiteful, deliberate, resolute, and confederate.

Over the psalm's reference the witnesses divide. The latin-fathers Augustine takes it wholly of Christ: the 'why' means 'in vain,' for what the persecutors wished, his destruction, they did not accomplish. Gill and Henry likewise read it chiefly of the Messiah and his enemies. But the reformed John Calvin sets David in the foreground as the literal subject and type: David boasts that his kingdom, though assailed by whole nations, will stand because upheld by God, and this — his throne being a shadow of the eternal kingdom truly established in Christ — is 'not violently, or even allegorically, applied to Christ, but was truly predicted concerning him.' The wesleyan-arminian voices agree: Adam Clarke supposes David composed it after taking Jerusalem and routing the confederate Philistines and their allies, David then typifying Christ and the psalm celebrating the Gospel's victories; John Wesley glosses the 'heathen' as those who raged against David in 2 Samuel 5 and against Christ in Acts 4:25. Ellicott, cautious about the occasion, lets the thought range from any historical prince to a larger and higher fulfilment, since 'the whole line of tradition claims the passage in a Messianic sense.'
2:
The rebellion now takes rank and file — 'the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together' — and the witnesses attend to the muster and its target. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the military sense: 'set themselves' means with hostile intent, as in Jeremiah 46:4, where the same word arrays warriors; the 'rulers' are properly grave dignitaries; and 'take counsel' is better 'have taken their plans, and are now mustering to carry them into effect.' He marks the change of tense — the poet first sees the array, then goes back to its origin — and lingers on 'against the LORD, and against his anointed,' where the word Messiah, applicable in its first sense to anyone anointed with holy oil in Leviticus 4:3, takes here its distinctive reference to the expected prince, a reference which, he judges, dates more from this psalm than from any other passage.

The reformed John Gill puts flesh on the kings: Herod the Great, who sought the child's life; Herod Antipas, who with his men of war mocked him; Pontius Pilate, who condemned him for the Roman emperor; and all the kings since who have persecuted Christ in his members and set themselves to hinder his Gospel. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley names the same pair, Herod and Pilate, and reads 'of the earth' as spoken in contempt, to show their madness in opposing the God of heaven; the anointed is the king whom God has chosen and exalted. Adam Clarke adds the Chaldee's rendering, 'against his Messiah,' and holds that the title, signifying the anointed person, refers first to David and secondly to Christ.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology of the alliance: it is against the Lord and against his anointed, that is, against all religion in general and the Christian religion in particular; and all who are enemies to Christ, whatever they pretend, are enemies to God himself, for, as the Lord said, 'they have hated both me and my Father.' The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lift the eye above the tumult to Jahve enthroned in the heavens, whose futures describe not what he will once do but what he does continually, controlling all that passes below with a power that brooks no hindrance. The voices converge: the confederacy is real and formidable, yet from the first line it is aimed, whether the plotters know it or not, at heaven itself.
3:
The mustered kings at last find their voice, and it is a cry for liberty from restraint — 'let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us.' The reformed John Gill is careful whose words these are: not the apostles or saints encouraging one another to throw off the yoke of Jewish ceremonies, but the heathen, the people, the kings and rulers, speaking with one voice against the Lord and his Anointed. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley hears in the second clause the same thing said with more emphasis: they would not merely break the yoke and the cords that fasten it, but fling them as far away as they can.

Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, finds here the very ground of the world's opposition, citing Bishop Horne: the unwillingness of rebellious nature to submit to the obligations of divine laws which cross men's interests and lay a restraint on their desires. 'Corrupt affections are the most inveterate enemies of Christ, and their language is, We will not have this man to reign over us. Doctrines would be readily believed if they involved no precepts; and the Church may be tolerated if she will only give up her discipline.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the movement of the poem at this point — the whispered purpose of the muttering nations now breaks out into loud menace, defiance passing along the ranks of the rebels — and notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate read 'yoke' for 'cords,' in keeping with the metaphor of a restive animal straining against the harness, as in Isaiah 10:27.

The latin-fathers Augustine reads the boast as spoken by those who 'meditate a vain thing': 'let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us' means, let us do our endeavour that the Christian religion not bind us nor be imposed upon us. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same sense into a diagnosis of the human heart: these are children of Belial who cannot endure the yoke, at least the yoke of the Lord and his anointed; yet the bands they strain against are 'cords of a man,' agreeable to right reason, and 'bands of love,' conducive to their true interest. Why do men oppose religion, he asks, but because they are impatient of its restraints? They would break asunder the bands of conscience and the cords of God's commandments, and cast them away as far from them as they can. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in this one sentence the whole quarrel of the rebel will with a government whose only tyranny is to command what is good.
4:
The scene shifts in an instant from the raging council-chamber to the calm of heaven, and the witnesses feel the deliberate contrast — 'he that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh.' The reformed John Gill reads the sitting as the point: God is enthroned above the kings of the earth, and his sitting still and quiet, serene and undisturbed, is set over against the running to and fro and the tumultuous assembling of the heathen; the laughter ascribed to him is spoken after the manner of men, by an anthropopathy, as he is elsewhere said to repent and grieve, and it shows how vain and fruitless their attempts must be against him and his Anointed. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the same note: Adam Clarke has him utterly contemn their puny efforts, beat down their pride, and confound their devices; John Wesley reads the sitting as that of the king of the whole world, whose seat in the heavens is evidence both of his certain knowledge of all done below and of his irresistible power, so that his laughter is to despise them and all their crafty devices.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls the turn a sublimity truly Hebrew: the psalm passes from the wild confusion on earth to the spectacle of God looking down with mingled scorn and wrath, and where we speak of the 'irony of events,' the Hebrew boldly ascribes the irony to God, who controls events. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the comfort out: he who sits in the heavens has such a prospect that he can oversee them all and all their projects, and such power that he can overcome them; the perfect repose of the Eternal Mind may be our comfort under all the disquietments of our own, for here God is said not to arise and stir himself but to sit still and vanquish them, since the utmost operations of his omnipotence cost him no difficulty and disturb not his eternal rest.

The latin-fathers Augustine alone refuses to let the laughter be read even figuratively of a face: nothing here must be taken in a carnal sort, as if God laughed with cheek or derided with nostril; the 'laughter' and 'derision' are the power he gives his saints, that, foreseeing how the name and rule of Christ shall pervade posterity and possess all nations, they may understand that the rebels 'meditate a vain thing.' The witnesses converge on the psalm's great reversal: the mightiest confederacy of earth is, to the God of heaven, no occasion for alarm but for a laughter that is itself a kind of judgment.
5:
The laughter does not stay silent; it hardens into speech and judgment — 'then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure.' The reformed John Gill reads the speaking as done not in God's word but in his providences, and not in love, as he chastises his own, but in great wrath inflicting just punishment; he refers it especially to the destruction of Jerusalem after the death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, when the Gospel, to the rulers' great mortification, had made large advances in the Gentile world. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the horizon: God spoke thus to the Jews who rejected the Gospel, ruining them by the Roman armies, and to the opposing Roman emperors, destroying the contending factions until he brought the empire under one head and converted him — Constantine — to Christianity.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the sound and the syntax. Charles Ellicott marks the emphatic particle 'then' as a climax, possibly equal to 'Lo! behold,' and hears in the original a grand roll of words like the roll of thunder, made more effective by its contrast with the quiet manner of the verse before; 'vex them' he renders more literally, greatly terrify them, the verb intensive, 'in his nostrils and in his heat.' Keil and Delitzsch feel the same violence: the verse is like a peal of thunder, and the phrase 'in his sore displeasure' like the lightning's destructive flash; as the first strophe closed with the words of the rebels, so this one closes with Jahve's own.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the mercy hidden in the terror. Though God despises the rebels as impotent, he does not therefore wink at them, but is justly displeased with them as impudent and impious; their sin is a real provocation, and his anger a real vexation, for if he do but speak to them in his wrath, the very breath of his mouth will be their confusion. As a word made us, Henry says, so a word can unmake us again; who knows the power of his anger? The enemies rage but cannot vex God, while God sits still and yet vexes them, bringing them to their wits' end — for his setting up the kingdom of his Son, in spite of them, is the greatest vexation of all. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in this thunderclap the settled truth that the God who laughs at rebellion will not laugh for ever, but speaks at last a word that undoes those who would not have his Son to reign.
6:
'Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion' — with this the LORD answers the whole confederacy in a single line, and the witnesses hear the accent fall on the defiant 'I.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the pronoun emphatic: 'You dare to revolt; it is I who have given this office to the king.' On the verb 'set' he opens a genuine question of rendering: literally it is 'poured out,' as of melted metal cast into a mould in Isaiah 40:19, whence the sense of establishing or setting up; but Gesenius and Ewald, following Symmachus, give the word the sense 'anointed,' which agrees well with the mention of the Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, rule that reading out: the Hebrew means to pour wide and firm, and so to set firmly in a place, as the Septuagint, Syriac, Jerome, and Luther all translate — the word for prince being comparable not to 'Messiah' but to one installed, set up by God's own hand.

The reformed John Gill turns to the hill itself: by Zion is meant the church of God, especially under the Gospel, so called because, like Zion, it is the object of God's love and choice, the place of his habitation, strongly fortified by his power and grace, immovable because built on Christ the Rock of ages, an high hill eminent and visible, and holy through the presence and worship of God and the sanctification of his Spirit. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads 'my king' as one who rules in God's stead, according to his will and for his glory, and takes Zion first strictly, the fortified hill called the city of David, then largely, for Jerusalem, the temple, the church of the Jews, and the Christian church.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse as the rebels' certain defeat, their counsels turned headlong. As David was advanced to the throne and made master of the stronghold of Zion despite the affronts of its garrison, so the Lord Jesus is exalted to the Father's right hand, head over all things to the church, notwithstanding the restless endeavours of his enemies. Christ took not this honour to himself but was called to it — 'I have set him, I have settled him' — and, being raised, is fixed; high places are slippery places, but this King stands. He is set upon Zion, the hill of God's holiness and a type of the gospel church, so that Christ's throne is set up in the hearts of all believers and in the societies they form. The witnesses do not divide: while the kings plot to keep the Anointed off the throne, God announces the coronation as a thing already done.
7:
'I will declare the decree' — now the Anointed himself takes up the word, and the witnesses hear a king rehearsing the charter of his reign. The reformed John Gill assigns the opening clause to Jehovah's Anointed exercising his kingly office, and is careful that 'the decree' relates to what precedes, the purpose of God concerning the Messiah and the salvation of his people, and not to the generation named next, which depends not on any decree or arbitrary will but is from the Son's very nature. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays the foundation deeper still: the Messiah's kingdom rests on an eternal decree of the Father, no sudden resolve nor trial of an experiment, but the result of the counsels of divine wisdom before all worlds, the federal transaction between Father and Son concerning man's redemption, declared now by a faithful witness who had lain in the Father's bosom from eternity.

Over 'this day have I begotten thee' the witnesses divide in earnest. Henry takes the words to refer both to the eternal generation itself, quoted in Hebrews 1:5 to prove Christ the express image of the Father, and to the demonstration of it by his resurrection, to which the apostle applies it in Acts 13:33. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will not allow the first sense at all: 'today' is an absolute designation of the present, excluding past and future, and can by no figure express eternity; 'begotten' here means manifested, exhibited, declared — Christ shown to be the Son of God with power by his resurrection, exactly as Paul argues in Romans 1:4. John Wesley holds the two readings side by side but leans as Clarke does, taking 'this day' either of the eternal generation, in which there is no yesterday or tomorrow but one continued day, or, as 'mainly intended,' of the manifestation of Christ's eternal sonship in time, chiefly at the resurrection.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the words on the coronation day of an anointed king, the great event making it as it were the new birthday of the monarch or the monarchy; the 'decree,' from a root meaning to engrave, is a formal ordinance announced by a prophet and legalised by the mutual adoption of king and people. From that particular prince — could we identify him — Ellicott lets the thought range on to a larger fulfilment, and grants that the whole line of tradition, with Hebrews 5:5 and 2 Samuel 7:14, claims the passage in a Messianic sense. The witnesses converge on the sonship even as they dispute the day: whether begotten from eternity, or declared by resurrection, or enthroned on Zion's hill, the King reigns as the Son of God.
8:
The decree passes into promise, and the Father invites the Son to name his inheritance — 'ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance.' The reformed John Gill hears in the 'ask' no inferiority but the intimacy of Father and Son: such a way of speaking shows the Father's great affection and the Son's sure interest, who could ask nothing but he had it. In the council and covenant of grace, Gill says, Christ asked for the persons of all the elect to be his bride, and for every blessing of grace for them, and the request of his lips was not withheld; here that same asking is promised its answer in a world-wide dominion, so that not the Jews only but the uttermost parts of the earth become his possession.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as the second branch of Christ's office, his mediatorial kingship: having died as an atoning sacrifice and risen, he now makes intercession, and in virtue of what he has done and suffered receives the nations for his inheritance and the uttermost parts of the earth for his possession, sending his apostles throughout the habitable globe to preach the Gospel to every man. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry frames the same as a title by agreement: the Son must ask, putting himself voluntarily into a state of inferiority by taking the human nature, and on that condition shall have the honour and power of a universal monarch. His government shall be universal — the heathen for his inheritance, not the Jews only, to whom the church had long been confined, but the Gentiles also, those in the uttermost parts of the earth; and this, begun when the Gentile world first received the Gospel, awaits its fuller accomplishment when the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdoms of the Lord and of his Christ in Revelation 11:15.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look beyond the promise to its close, where the poet turns from what he has seen and heard to a practical application to the great of the earth. The 'judges of the earth,' they note, are not those who judge the earth but the rulers belonging to it, throughout its length and breadth, and the exhortation is addressed not to the rebels alone but to kings in general, in the light of what the seer has prophetically beheld. The witnesses do not divide: the Son's inheritance is the very nations that raged, and the asking that secures it is at once the intercession by which he saves them and the claim by which he reigns.
9:
The promised dominion has a stern edge — 'thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel' — and the witnesses take care to say whom the rod falls on. The reformed John Gill distinguishes sharply: not the inheritance given him among the Gentiles, whom Christ delights in and preserves, but the stubborn and rebellious who will not have him reign over them, who despise his government and his Gospel; toward these he will exert his power and break them in pieces. Gill notes the rendering of the Septuagint and other versions, 'shall rule' or 'feed them,' and reconciles it: understood of the strictness of his justice, without the least display of mercy, 'shall rule' comes to the same as 'shall break.'

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays the same variant bare. The Septuagint translated 'thou shalt pasture them,' taking the rod as a shepherd's crook, as in Leviticus 27:32; elsewhere the rod is a sceptre in Psalms 125:3, and in Proverbs 22:15 a rod of correction. But the use to be made of it — to dash the nations in pieces as one breaks a potter's vessel — points, he judges, to the last of these senses, and he quotes Milton's version of the iron sceptre that bruises and disperses. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the breaking historically. Adam Clarke refers it to the Jewish nation, whose rejection of the Gospel was foreseen: dispossessed of their land, their city razed, their temple burnt, and a great multitude slaughtered by the Romans, so heavily did the iron rod of God's judgments fall for their unbelief. John Wesley agrees that those who will not submit are crushed, fulfilled in part when the unbelieving Jews were destroyed by the Roman power and again in the fall of the Pagan power, but not completely 'till all opposing power and principality be put down.'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the doctrine of it. The same event is foretold in Daniel 2:40, where the Roman power is the kingdom of iron; and the rebels are but a potter's vessel before Christ, suddenly, easily, and irreparably dashed, as in Revelation 2:27. 'Thou shalt do it,' Henry paraphrases — thou shalt have leave and power to do it, and shalt do it effectually; nations shall be ruined rather than the gospel church go unbuilt. The witnesses do not divide over the sense, only over the reach: whether the iron rod fell chiefly on unbelieving Jerusalem, or on Pagan Rome, or waits still for the final subduing of every opposing power; and all agree that those who will not bow to the golden sceptre shall break beneath the iron one.
10:
With the judgment declared, the psalm turns to plead, and the witnesses hear a summons of mercy in it — 'be wise now therefore, O ye kings; be instructed, ye judges of the earth.' The reformed John Gill takes the address to reach beyond David's day to the kings under the Gospel who would set themselves against the Lord and his Anointed, and their subjects with them; they are called to be wise, for great men are not always wise, and to rise up against the Messiah is folly, since there is no counsel against the Lord. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens it to the rulers of all kingdoms, nations, and states, who should listen to the Gospel's maxims and govern by its precepts; 'be instructed,' he urges, is rather 'be reformed' — cast away all idolatrous maxims and receive the Gospel as the basis of the law of the land.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as the practical application of the whole gospel doctrine of Christ's kingdom. He that has power to destroy the rebels shows that he takes no pleasure in their destruction, for he puts them in a way to make themselves happy; and kings and judges, who give law and judgment to others, must themselves receive law from Christ, standing before God on a level with the meanest of their subjects. What is said to them, Henry adds, is said to all, and directed to kings only because of the influence their example has upon their inferiors, and because it was men of rank and power who had opposed the setting up of Christ's kingdom.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording and the sweep. Keil and Delitzsch read the connecting 'now therefore' as drawing a practical conclusion from all the seer has beheld, addressed not to the rebels he saw but to kings in general; the 'judges of the earth' are its rulers throughout its breadth, and the verbs bid them show discernment and let themselves be admonished. Charles Ellicott notes that here begins the psalm's fourth and closing section, in which subject princes are warned, as a religious duty no less than a political necessity, to submit in time; and he recalls, as a historical curiosity, that the words 'et nunc reges intelligite' — now be wise, O ye kings — formed the legend of the medal struck in England after the execution of Charles I. The witnesses do not divide: the God who could crush the kings stoops instead to counsel them, and the same power that threatens the rod holds out the offer of wisdom.
11:
The counsel becomes command, and the witnesses weigh how fear and joy can be yoked in a single breath — 'serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.' The reformed John Gill takes the service to be rendered to the true Jehovah alone, Father, Son, and Spirit, and not to the idols of the Gentiles; the kings and judges are not thereby required to lay aside their crowns and sceptres and turn preachers, but to serve God in the discharge of their office according to his will. The wesleyan-arminian voices set the two affections together: Adam Clarke bids them fear God with the reverence due to his supreme majesty and serve him as subjects their sovereign, yet, serving him aright, they cannot but be happy — only let a continual filial fear moderate all their joys, since they must stand at last before his judgment-seat. John Wesley reads the fear as an awful sense of God's great and glorious majesty, and the rejoicing as the refusal to esteem his yoke a grievance; the trembling is added to warn them not to turn this grace of God into wantonness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the two duties perfectly consistent. God is great and holy and provoked against us, and therefore to be feared; yet he is our Lord and benefactor, and therefore to be rejoiced in — even kings, whom others serve and fear, must serve and fear him, for there is the same infinite distance between them and God as between the meanest subject and him. We must rejoice, Henry says, in the setting up of Christ's kingdom, but rejoice with a holy awe, a fear for ourselves lest we come short; our salvation must be wrought out with fear and trembling, as in Philippians 2:12, and whatever we rejoice in must be held with trembling, lest we grow vain in our joy — to rejoice with trembling is to rejoice as though we rejoiced not, as in 1 Corinthians 7:30.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the surprising word: 'rejoice with trembling' is more literally 'quake,' the motion of the body produced by strong emotion, and so used both of joy and of terror. The old versions, he notes, shrank from the boldness and paraphrased it — the Chaldee 'pray,' the Syriac 'cleave to him,' the Arabic 'praise him' — where the Authorized Version, following the Septuagint, keeps the trembling. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the homage due to the enthroned Son is neither a servile dread that cannot rejoice nor a careless joy that will not tremble, but a reverent gladness in which the two are one.
12:
'Kiss the Son, lest he be angry' — the psalm's closing charge is also its most disputed line, and the witnesses gather around a single Aramaic word. The reformed John Gill retains the familiar sense: the 'Son' is the Son of God named in v.7, the word coming from a root that signifies to choose and to purify, so that he is God's elect and the pure One; and to kiss him is to render the love due to one lovely above all creatures, the homage of subjects to their king, and the adoration owed to God. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way — kiss the Son of God in token of subjection and adoration, a sign among the eastern nations — and glosses 'ye perish' as being taken out of the way by death or destruction, for the least degree of his anger is terrible.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott holds that 'this familiar translation must be surrendered.' It has against it the weight of all the ancient versions but the Syriac — the Chaldee 'receive instruction,' the Septuagint and Vulgate 'lay hold of discipline,' Symmachus and Jerome 'pay pure adoration'; the word 'bar' for 'son' is Aramaic, occurring in Hebrew only in Proverbs 31:2, and the psalmist had just used the native 'ben' in v.7, so that the abrupt 'kiss son' is too bald even for Hebrew poetry, while the change of subject to 'lest he' — meaning Jehovah — is awkward. His most consistent rendering is therefore 'proffer pure homage' to the LORD, and he ranks the current of Rabbinical and modern authority behind him, from 'arm yourselves with discipline' to Hupfeld's 'yield sincerely' and Ewald's 'receive wholesome warning.' The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans the same way: 'bar' being a Chaldee word in so pure a Hebrew poem, and the versions reading 'doctrine' or 'discipline,' he takes it as 'embrace that which is pure, namely, the doctrine of God,' kissing being the token of subjection and friendship.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps 'Kiss the Son' and unfolds it as the great duty of the Christian religion: a kiss not of betrayal, as Judas gave, but of reconciliation, of adoration and religious worship, of sincere affection, and of allegiance, taking Christ's yoke and giving oneself to be governed by his laws. The reasons, Henry says, are drawn from our own interest — 'lest he be angry,' for if we slight the Mediator the Father's wrath abides on us by John 3:36, with the Son's added; and 'lest ye perish from the way,' going to hell from the very way to heaven. Yet the psalm ends not in terror but in benediction, on the word Clarke marks as the same that opened the Psalter in Psalms 1:1: 'blessed are all they that put their trust in him' — or, as Ellicott renders it, that find their refuge in him. So the witnesses close where they divide, some hearing 'kiss the Son' and some 'do homage,' yet all agreeing that the psalm which began with rebellion ends with the one wisdom of submission, and that good must at last triumph over evil, the rebels conquered by being drawn in.
